```{r app, eval = FALSE}
shiny::runApp(happiness_app(

))
```
## Analyse the data

### Research question

The World Happiness Report identifies social support as one of the main
factors associated with differences in happiness between countries
[@helliwell2023]. We examine whether this association varies across
continents, while accounting for differences in GDP.

Does the relationship between social support and happiness differ between
continents, after controlling for Logged GDP per capita?

### Data and method

We use country-level happiness data from the World Happiness Report 2023
[@helliwell2023; @singh2023]. Happiness is the outcome, social support is
the primary predictor, continent is the moderator, and Logged GDP per
capita is the control variable.

We fit a linear regression with an interaction between social support and
continent. This allows the association between social support and happiness
to differ between continents. The overall interaction test evaluates whether
these differences improve the model compared with a model without the
interaction.

We use HC3 robust standard errors, which allow the residual spread to vary
between countries [@long2000]. Countries with missing or nonfinite values
are excluded. Continents with fewer than five countries with complete
data are also excluded.

Analyses were run in R [@rcoreteam2026], using HC3 standard errors from
the sandwich package [@zeileis2004] and robust tests from the lmtest
package [@zeileis2002]. Continents were assigned using the countrycode
package [@arelbundock2018].

```{r analysis}
social_support_result <- analyse_happiness(
  primary_predictor = "Social support",
  moderator = "continent",
  control_variables = "Logged GDP per capita"
)
```

### Visualisation

The points represent the observed happiness scores of individual countries.
Each continent has its own fitted line and 95% confidence band. For these
predictions, Logged GDP per capita is held at its mean across the countries
included in the analysis. The points are not adjusted for GDP, so they need
not be centred around their continent's line. For example, countries with
above-average GDP may sit above the line because the line assumes average
GDP. The lines are restricted to the social support values observed within
each continent.

```{r analysis-plot, fig.width=9, fig.height=6}
plot_happiness(social_support_result)
```

### Results

The coefficient table shows the estimated associations and their confidence
intervals. Africa is the reference continent. The social support coefficient
is the estimated association between social support and happiness in Africa,
after controlling for Logged GDP per capita. Interaction coefficients show
how the slopes of the other continents differ from the slope in Africa.

```{r analysis-coefficients}
knitr::kable(format_coefficients(social_support_result))
```

The relationship between social support and happiness differs between
continents after controlling for Logged GDP per capita. The overall robust
Wald test gives $$F(4, 124) = 5.97$$, $$p < .001$$.

The estimated slopes are approximately 6.3 in Europe and 6.1 in Asia,
indicating stronger positive associations in these continents. The estimated
slope in Africa is 1.15, with a confidence interval that includes zero.
The estimated slopes are approximately 0.75 in North America and 3.0 in
South America. North and South America include only 11 and 10 countries,
respectively, so their estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

These findings suggest that social support is not equally strongly
associated with happiness across continents. However, they do not establish
why these differences occur. Differences in other country characteristics,
not fully captured by GDP, could contribute to the observed pattern.

```{r analysis-results, results='asis'}
cat(
  paste(describe_result(social_support_result), collapse = "\n\n"),
  "\n"
)
```

### Limitations

These are observational, country-level associations. They do not establish
causation or show that the same relationships hold for individuals.
Adjusting for GDP does not remove all possible confounding.

This analysis addresses one of many questions that can be explored with
the app, so the findings should be treated as exploratory rather than
confirmatory.

Oceania was excluded because only two countries had complete data, below
the minimum of five. North America and South America included only 11 and
10 countries, respectively, making their slope estimates imprecise.
HC3 standard errors allow unequal residual spread but do not correct for
spatial dependence between countries.

## Assumption checks

The regression assumptions are checked for every predictor in the simple
model happiness ~ predictor (README, Methods). The counts:

```{r assumption-checks}
assumption_checks <- check_assumptions()
knitr::kable(assumption_checks$summary)
```

We assess spatial dependence in the residuals using Moran's I, comparing
models with and without continent as a control [@moran1950]:

```{r spatial}
knitr::kable(assumption_checks$spatial, digits = 3)
```

For selected predictors, we include continent as a control and calculate
standard errors clustered by continent [@zeileis2020]. These are robustness
checks for separate models, not the moderation model above. Interpret them
cautiously because the number of clusters is small:

```{r clustered}
knitr::kable(assumption_checks$clustered, digits = 3)
```
